recentItems.title: Former Mexican Mafia Rene “Boxer” Enriquez on Joining Gang at 12, 1st Drive-By at 14 (Part 1)
recentItems.description:

--------
Former Mexican Mafia member Rene “Boxer” Enriquez sits down with VladTV to discuss his early life in Cerritos, California, and the path that led him from a working-class family into Artesia 13 as a child. Enriquez explains how his older brother Mark influenced him, how he says he was “jumped in” at just 12 years old, and how gang rivalries with Hawaiian Gardens, Norwalk, and other Los Angeles-area neighborhoods escalated into violence. He recalls the killing of a homeboy at El Dorado Park, retaliatory shootings, and participating in his first drive-by around age 14. Enriquez also breaks down the meaning of “13,” its connection to the Mexican Mafia, and the culture surrounding Southern California street gangs. Convicted of two murders before becoming a federal informant in 2002, Enriquez offers a firsthand account of gang life, loyalty, violence, and consequence.

In this VladTV interview, Lil Jungle Boy reflects on his early years in Los Angeles, joining the Bloods, and the violence that followed after the death of his brother Big Bulldog, who he says was killed by police. He describes life around MLK, Crenshaw Mall, Buckingham and Hillcrest, including tense encounters with rivals, hustling, and moving through different neighborhoods.

The conversation centers on the day Lil Jungle Boy says he was shot in the head during a police stop after a shooting near Tasty Q’s. He recalls driving a Monte Carlo SS, carrying a Sidekick XL phone, and being fired on after reaching for it despite saying he was unarmed. He also explains why the bullet remains in his head and discusses Officer Whiteman, the Southwest Gang Unit investigation, and how it later affected his legal case.

--------
In this VladTV full interview, William Noguera recounts his path from La Puente car thief and martial arts fighter to one of California’s youngest men sentenced to death. Convicted for a 1983 Orange County murder at age 18, Noguera spent 42 years behind bars, much of it inside San Quentin’s death row, where he crossed paths with Stanley “Tookie” Williams, Richard Ramirez, Joseph Naso, Lawrence Bittaker and other notorious inmates.

Noguera discusses prison politics, the Mexican Mafia, execution dates, California’s death penalty system, Gavin Newsom’s role in parole reviews, and his eventual release after a unanimous parole decision. He also details how conversations with serial killers led to his book *Through the Lens of a Monster* and Peacock’s *Death Row Confidential: Secrets of a Serial Killer*. A candid look at violence, remorse, justice, and survival.

#WilliamNoguera #VladTV #DeathRow #SanQuentin #TrueCrime

Part 1: https://youtu.be/byG2_0gACAg
--------
Charleston White addresses the online rumor that he was evicted, explaining his side of a disputed lease-to-buy deal involving an $800,000 home, a $20,000 down payment, alleged property liens, and a realtor he claims had a suspended license. White says the situation escalated after the house was broken into while he was on tour, with unresolved damage to the back door, questions about who had access, and a police report tied to the incident.

He also names Santana, described as Trick Daddy’s former manager, while detailing concerns about a Colombian girlfriend, workers coming in and out of the property, a non-English-speaking pool boy, flooding near the pool area, and mildew issues inside the home. Rather than framing it as a simple eviction, Charleston says he stopped paying rent on advice tied to the dispute and is letting his attorney fight the matter in court.

G. Dep closes out his VladTV interview with a Harlem hip-hop “This or That” bracket, weighing legends and icons including Kurtis Blow, Kool Moe Dee, Doug E. Fresh, Herb McGruff, Smoke DZA, 40 Cal, J.R. Writer, Dave East, Diddy, Jim Jones, Max B, A$AP Ferg, A$AP Rocky, Big L, Juelz Santana, Ma$e, and Cam’ron. After repeatedly backing Doug E. Fresh as the ultimate entertainer, G. Dep switches when Black Rob enters the matchup—and rides with his late friend to the end, calling him the top choice among Harlem rappers.

The conversation then turns reflective as Vlad acknowledges G. Dep’s decision to take accountability for his past, serve time in prison, get clean, and remain committed to sobriety. G. Dep also shares gratitude, mentions his upcoming book, and pays respect to Black Rob’s lasting legacy.
